info.bio: Formando un poderoso trío con sus hermanos en los 50's, Wray produjo un vulgar, violento y siniestro sonido como nadie antes había escuchado hasta la fecha. Basando a menudo sus instrumentales en acordes rítmicos, Wray fue llamado a la vez "El abuelo de los power chords" y "El padre del Heavy-Metal". Aunque su popularidad tuvo una corta vida, su estilo permaneció en las guitarras de Pete Townshend, Jeff Beck, y Jimmy Page, y días después en las cuerdas de los practicantes del heavy-metal, punk y grunge.

scenes.name: Los rockers de garaje
scenes.author: Jon Savage
scenes.desc: En 1966 no tenían nombre (Billboard los llamaba «rockers»); hoy se les llama grupos de garaje. La respuesta creativa americana a la invasión británica: chicos blancos de suburbio que ensayaban en el garaje familiar y tocaban en gimnasios, iglesias y fiestas, con cortes de pelo de Brian Jones, actitud de Jagger, fuzz, rave-ups a lo Yardbirds, Them y Stones y, casi siempre, un órgano Farfisa o Vox con un regusto siniestro de película de terror de autocine. Recuperaban la línea del rock americano de 1963-1964 (Kingsmen, Trashmen) que los Beatles cortaron en seco: «Hanky Panky» de Tommy James, grabado en 1963, fue número 1 en julio de 1966. Ese septiembre las listas se llenaron de discos duros: «96 Tears» de ? and the Mysterians (mexicanoamericanos de Flint, con un órgano hipnótico de otro disco), «Dirty Water» de los Standells, «You’re Gonna Miss Me» de los 13th Floor Elevators y «Psychotic Reaction» de Count Five, calco del «I’m a Man» de los Yardbirds. Quejas dirigidas a las mujeres, pero también una nueva confianza; quejas pequeñas que empezaban a encontrar un objetivo, como en «One of These Days» de los Roosters.

scenes.name: Antes del diluvio
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: La «edad oscura» del rock'n'roll: los rebeldes son sustituidos por ídolos adolescentes educados y el Brill Building devuelve el poder a los compositores profesionales. Pero en esos años se incuban la revolución futura: la guitarra fuzz de Link Wray, los bailes de moda (el twist), el rock instrumental de guitarras (Duane Eddy, Ventures, Shadows), el calipso y el primer ska, el doo-wop más inventivo (Coasters, Drifters, Five Royales), el nacimiento del soul (Sam Cooke, Ray Charles, Motown, Stax), el estudio como instrumento de Joe Meek y el surf de los Beach Boys y del «muro de sonido» de Phil Spector.

podcast.title: Band Influence for The Cramps
podcast.body: Link Wray was mentioned as an influence for The Cramps, among other rockabilly and early rock and roll artists, reflecting their interest in the raw, primitive sounds of the 1950s. "También eran influencias para la banda Ricky Nelson, Roy Orbson, Jassie Latkins o Lingray."

podcast.title: Cherokee WWII Veteran
podcast.body: Link Wray was an Indigenous Cherokee veteran of World War II, a detail that underscores his unique background and individualistic approach to music. "Link Wright, meterano indígena Cherokee de la Segunda Guerra Mundial."

podcast.title: DIY Amplifier Distortion
podcast.body: To achieve his signature savage sound, Link Wray deliberately perforated the cones of his amplifier. This was an innovative technique, as amplifiers at the time did not have built-in distortion regulation, which was not their intended purpose, leading him to create that ragged, menacing, and deeply physical tone. "Y para sonar así de salvaje, el lo que hizo fue perforar los colos de su amplificador, consiguiendo ese tono rasgado, amenazante y profundamente físico."

podcast.title: First Instrumental Song Censored
podcast.body: "Rumble" was the first and only time an instrumental piece was censored for its symbolic content. Several radio stations in the United States banned the song, arguing that its sound, despite having no words, could incite youth violence, highlighting its perceived dangerousness. "Fue la primera y única vez que una pieza instrumental era censurada por su carga simbólica."

podcast.title: Influence on Guitar Legends
podcast.body: His innovative guitar playing style, particularly his use of power chords, directly influenced iconic guitarists such as Jimmy Page and Pete Townshend, who picked up the guitar in part because of his sound. "Jimmy Page, Pete Townsend, guys like that picked up the guitar in part because of Link Ray."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Inventor of the Power Chord
podcast.body: Link Wray is credited with popularizing the idea of playing power chords on an electric guitar, a technique that would profoundly influence rock music. He is often called the "inventor of the power cord." "He has been called the inventor of the power cord, Jimmy Page, Pete Townsend, guys like that picked up the guitar in part because of Link Ray."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Shawnee Heritage Obscured
podcast.body: Link Wray was born in North Carolina to parents from the Shawnee tribe, making him a Native American. However, census documents of the time identified him as white, obscuring his true ethnicity. "His name was Link Ray, and he was born in North Carolina to parents from the Shawnee tribe. But that ethnicity was obscured by census documents that identified him as white, but he was definitely Native American."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Speaker Cone Alteration
podcast.body: In 1958, Link Wray, inspired by messing around with a damaged amplifier, started intentionally poking holes in the speaker cones of his own amp. This technique was used to achieve a raspy, loved sound for his instrumental track "Rumble." "He started poking holes in the speaker cones of his amp to make them sound all raspy."
